title: Cleaning your data: quality control
text:
Real genotype data is never perfect: some variants are poorly measured, some samples have too much missing data, and a few errors always slip in. Quality control (QC) removes these problems before any analysis, so that later results are trustworthy.
In this section you will apply a few standard filters, one at a time. After each one you will look at a number in the log file to confirm it worked — so you always know you are on track.
Every PLINK command writes a .log file (named after whatever you put in --out). That log is where you check your work — it is plain text, and you can open it with head, cat, or any text editor.

title: Cleaning your data: quality control
text:
Step 1 — Remove poorly genotyped variants
Why. Some variants failed to be measured in many individuals (a low “call rate”). A variant missing in too many people is unreliable, so we drop it. The --geno filter removes variants missing in more than a chosen fraction of samples (here, 2%).
Run this:
plink2 --bfile pdac_gwas_demo_full --geno 0.02 --make-bed --out qc_step1






Tip✅ Check your work



Open qc_step1.log and look for this line:
--geno: 8480 variants removed due to missing genotype data.
If you see 8480 variants removed, you did it right — those are exactly the poorly genotyped variants built into the demo data.

title: Cleaning your data: quality control
text:
Step 2 — Remove poorly genotyped samples
Why. The same problem can affect individuals: some samples have too much missing data across all their variants, which usually signals a low-quality sample. The --mind filter removes individuals missing more than a chosen fraction of their genotypes.
Run this (note we now start from the cleaned file qc_step1):
plink2 --bfile qc_step1 --mind 0.02 --make-bed --out qc_step2






Tip✅ Check your work



Open qc_step2.log and look for:
--mind: 25 samples removed due to missing genotype data.
25 samples removed means success — those are the low-quality samples deliberately added to the demo data.

title: Cleaning your data: quality control
section: Step 3 — Remove rare variants by minor allele frequency (MAF)
text:
Step 3 — Remove rare variants by minor allele frequency (MAF)
Why. Very rare variants (carried by only a handful of people) give unstable, unreliable association results in a study of this size. We remove variants whose minor allele frequency is below a threshold — here 1% (--maf 0.01).
Run this:
plink2 --bfile qc_step2 --maf 0.015 --make-bed --out qc_step3






Tip✅ Check your work



Open qc_step3.log and look for a line like:
<NNN> variants removed due to allele frequency threshold(s)
  (--maf/--max-maf/--mac/--max-mac).
You should see roughly [NNN] variants removed. (Exact number to be locked in from one real run — see note at the bottom.)

title: Cleaning your data: quality control
section: Step 4 — Remove variants failing Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Step 4 — Remove variants failing Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
Why. A strong departure from Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (the expected balance of genotypes in a population) often points to a genotyping error rather than real biology. We remove variants whose departure is extreme (--hwe with a strict p-value cutoff).
Run this:
plink2 --bfile qc_step3 --hwe 1e-6 --make-bed --out qc_step4






Tip✅ Check your work



Open qc_step4.log and look for:
--hwe: <NNN> variants removed due to Hardy-Weinberg exact test p-value threshold.
You should see about [NNN] variants removed. (Exact number to be locked in from one real run.)

title: Cleaning your data: quality control
section: Step 5 — Check that recorded sex matches the genetic data
text:
Step 5 — Check that recorded sex matches the genetic data
Why. A useful sanity check is whether each person’s recorded sex matches the sex inferred from their X chromosome. A mismatch usually means a sample mix-up. This check reports problems rather than removing data automatically.
Run this:
plink --bfile qc_step4 --check-sex --out qc_sexcheck






Tip✅ Check your work



Count the flagged samples in the result:
grep PROBLEM qc_sexcheck.sexcheck
You should find 4 samples flagged as PROBLEM — exactly the four sex discordances built into the demo data. In a real study you would investigate and usually remove these.

title: Cleaning your data: quality control
text:
Putting it together
Once you understand each filter, you can apply them in a single command:
plink2 --bfile pdac_gwas_demo_full \
       --geno 0.02 --mind 0.02 --maf 0.01 --hwe 1e-6 \
       --make-bed --out pdac_gwas_demo_qc
The result, pdac_gwas_demo_qc, is your cleaned dataset — the starting point for the next sections.






NoteWhy we filter one step at a time first



Running the filters separately lets you see how many variants or samples each one removes — which is how you catch a problem early. The order can slightly change the final counts, so for reproducible results always report the exact commands and thresholds you used.









ImportantA note on the exact numbers



The counts above for call rate (8,480 variants), sample missingness (25 samples), and sex check (4 samples) are the artefacts deliberately built into the demo dataset, so they are the targets to confirm. The MAF and HWE removal counts depend on the exact thresholds and on filter order, so they are shown as placeholders. Run the pipeline once on the demo data and the precise numbers will appear in the logs — drop them in here (or share the .log) and the check boxes can state the exact figures.

title: Before you start: setup and your first PLINK command
text: This page gets your computer ready and walks you through your very first command. By the end you will have downloaded the demo dataset, installed PLINK, and run a quick test that confirms everything works — computing allele frequencies with --freq.
crumbs: Before you start: setup and your first PLINK command

title: Before you start: setup and your first PLINK command
section: A note on the command line
text:
A note on the command line
Most steps in this guide are typed into a terminal (also called a “command line” or “console”) — a window where you type a command, press Enter, and the program runs.

Windows: open the Command Prompt (search for cmd) or PowerShell.
macOS: open the Terminal app (in Applications → Utilities).
Linux: open your Terminal.
Inside RStudio: there is a Terminal tab next to the Console tab — you can use that too.

Throughout the guide, lines you type into the terminal look like this:
plink2 --version
You copy the command, paste it into your terminal, and press Enter. That’s it.
crumbs: Before you start: setup and your first PLINK command

title: Before you start: setup and your first PLINK command
text:
Step 1 — Download the demo dataset
The demo dataset is called pdac_demo. Like all PLINK datasets, it is made of three files that always travel together and must stay in the same folder:







File
What it contains




pdac_demo.bed
the genotypes (the actual genetic data, in compact binary form)


pdac_demo.bim
the list of variants (one row per SNP: chromosome, position, alleles)


pdac_demo.fam
the list of individuals (one row per person: ID, sex, case/control status)









Important



Never rename or move just one of the three files. PLINK always looks for all three together using the shared name (pdac_demo).


You can download them in either of two ways.

Check the files arrivedOptional: read it in R


In your terminal, move into the folder and list its contents:
cd path/to/gwas_tutorial      # replace with the real path to your folder
ls pdac_demo.*      # on Windows Command Prompt use: dir pdac_demo.*
You should see exactly three files: .bed, .bim and .fam.


Step 2 — Install PLINK 2
PLINK is the workhorse program for genotype data. We use PLINK 2 (the command is plink2). It is a single program file — there is no installer: you download it, unzip it, and you are done.

Go to the official download page: https://www.cog-genomics.org/plink/2.0/
Download the build for your operating system (Linux / macOS / Windows).
Unzip it. Inside you will find the program file: plink2 (macOS/Linux) or plink2.exe (Windows).







TipThe simplest setup



Put the plink2 (or plink2.exe) file in the same folder as your data (gwas_tutorial). Then you can run it as ./plink2 (macOS/Linux) or plink2 (Windows) without worrying about installation paths. More advanced users can instead add PLINK to their system PATH.



macOS / LinuxWindows


If you placed plink2 in your working folder, you call it with ./plink2. The first time on macOS you may need to allow it to run:
chmod +x plink2          # make the file executable
./plink2 --version


Open Command Prompt, move to your folder, and call it as plink2:
cd path\to\gwas_tutorial
plink2 --version









Noteplink2 vs ./plink2



For the rest of this guide we write the command simply as plink2. On macOS/Linux, if PLINK is in your current folder rather than installed system-wide, type ./plink2 instead. Everything after the program name is identical.





Step 3 — Check that PLINK runs
Before doing anything with the data, confirm PLINK starts at all:
plink2 --version
You should see a single line with the version and build date, similar to:
PLINK v2.0.0-a.6.9 64-bit (1 Mar 2025)
If you see a version line, PLINK works. If instead you get an error like command not found or 'plink2' is not recognized, jump to Troubleshooting below.



Step 4 — Your first command: allele frequencies with --freq
Now the real test. We ask PLINK to read the demo dataset and compute the allele frequency of every variant — that is, how common each allele is across the sample. This is the simplest possible operation that touches the actual genotypes, so it is a perfect “does everything work?” check.
plink2 --bfile pdac_demo --freq --out pdac_demo_freq
Let’s read that command piece by piece:







Part
Meaning




plink2
run the PLINK 2 program


--bfile pdac_demo
load the dataset whose three files share this name (.bed/.bim/.fam)


--freq
compute the allele frequencies


--out pdac_demo_freq
name the output files with this prefix



CODE 0-01: first PLINK run — allele frequencies — see /getting_started/
When it finishes, PLINK prints a short log to the screen and creates a new file: pdac_demo_freq.afreq. The on-screen log ends with something like:
... 
430000 variants loaded from pdac_demo.bim.
1461 samples (712 females, 749 males; ...) loaded from pdac_demo.fam.
--freq: Allele frequencies written to pdac_demo_freq.afreq .
If you see a line saying the allele frequencies were written, the test has passed: PLINK can read your data and compute on it. 🎉



Step 5 — Did it work? Look at the result
Open the first few lines of the output file to see what PLINK produced:
head pdac_demo_freq.afreq    # on Windows use: more pdac_demo_freq.afreq
You should see a table with one row per variant, like this:
#CHROM  ID                REF  ALT  ALT_FREQS   OBS_CT
1       1:752566:G:A      G    A    0.831621    2922
1       1:776546:A:C      A    C    0.142847    2922
1       1:832918:T:C      T    C    0.067419    2922
1       1:842013:T:G      T    G    0.219370    2922
...
What the columns mean:







Column
Meaning




#CHROM
chromosome


ID
the variant’s identifier


REF / ALT
the reference and alternate alleles


ALT_FREQS
frequency of the ALT allele (a number between 0 and 1)


OBS_CT
number of observed alleles (≈ 2 × number of genotyped individuals)



That ALT_FREQS column is the answer to our test: PLINK computed a frequency for every variant.



If you have R/RStudio set up, you can load the same file and take a quick look. This also introduces the pattern we use throughout the guide — PLINK produces a table, R reads and summarises it:

# read the allele-frequency table PLINK just wrote
freq <- read.table("pdac_demo_freq.afreq",
                   header = TRUE, comment.char = "", sep = "\t",
                   check.names = FALSE)

# how many variants, and the first rows
nrow(freq)
head(freq)

# minor allele frequency (MAF) = the smaller of ALT_FREQS and 1 - ALT_FREQS
freq$MAF <- pmin(freq$ALT_FREQS, 1 - freq$ALT_FREQS)

# a quick picture of the frequency spectrum
hist(freq$MAF, breaks = 50,
     main = "Minor allele frequency distribution",
     xlab = "MAF")

A typical genotyping array shows many common variants and a tail of rarer ones, so the histogram leans toward the lower MAF values. If R prints a number of variants and draws a histogram, your R setup works too — and you are ready for the analysis sections.






NoteWhy we don’t re-run PLINK every time the website is built



Real GWAS commands (especially on full datasets) can be slow and run on a dedicated server. In this guide, PLINK commands are shown for you to run on your own machine; the website does not re-execute them. Lightweight R steps (a plot, a small table) are run once and cached, so the site stays fast and reproducible.




Troubleshooting






Warningcommand not found / 'plink2' is not recognized





The terminal cannot find the PLINK program. Either you are not in the folder where plink2 lives, or it is not on your PATH.

Make sure you have cd-ed into your working folder.
On macOS/Linux, call it as ./plink2 (note the ./).
Check the file is really there: ls plink2 (macOS/Linux) or dir plink2.exe (Windows).










WarningError: Failed to open pdac_demo.bed





PLINK cannot find the data files.

Confirm all three files (.bed, .bim, .fam) are in the current folder and share the exact name pdac_demo.
Confirm you typed the name without an extension after --bfile (PLINK adds .bed/.bim/.fam itself).
Check you are in the right folder with pwd (macOS/Linux) or cd with no arguments (Windows).










WarningmacOS: “plink2 cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified”





This is macOS Gatekeeper. Either right-click the plink2 file → Open once to allow it, or run xattr -d com.apple.quarantine plink2 in the terminal, then try again.






What’s next
You now have a working setup and have confirmed PLINK can read the demo data. The next sections of the guide build directly on this:

Quality control (Section 1B) — cleaning the raw genotypes before any analysis.
Population stratification (Section 2) — detecting and correcting for ancestry.

(These sections will be linked here as they are added.)

title: Contributing
text:
Thank you for contributing to the GWAS guide. This file explains how we work together so that everyone builds on the same, consistent base of files.
The golden rule: main is protected. It always reflects the agreed, harmonised version. You never commit directly to it — you propose changes through a Pull Request (PR), which a maintainer reviews and merges.
Maintainers (the only people who merge to main): Manuel Gentiluomo and Riccardo Farinella.



# clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/<OWNER>/how-to-gwas-pdac.git
cd how-to-gwas-pdac

# tell git who you are (so your contributions are attributed correctly)
git config user.name  "Your Name"
git config user.email "your.email@institution.edu"
If you do not yet have write access, ask Manuel to add you as a collaborator, or fork the repository and open PRs from your fork.





Sync with the latest main before starting:
git checkout main
git pull
Create a branch for your work. Use the convention section<NN>-<short-topic>:
git checkout -b section02-pca-draft
Work inside your section folder (sections/<your section>/). Add your Markdown text and your annotated scripts there. Do not edit other people’s sections without coordinating first.
Commit in small, clear steps:
git add sections/02_population_stratification/
git commit -m "Section 2: first draft of PCA narrative + plink2 PCA script"
Push your branch and open a Pull Request to main:
git push -u origin section02-pca-draft
Then open the PR on GitHub and request review from a maintainer.
A maintainer reviews, may ask for small edits, and merges. After merge, delete your branch and start the next piece from a fresh main.


Working on the same files at the same time? Pull often and keep branches short-lived to avoid conflicts.






Languages/tools: PLINK 2 and R only, unless agreed otherwise.
One step = one script, numbered, self-contained, and heavily commented — remember the audience has no bioinformatics background. A reader should understand why each flag/option is used, not just what it does.
Every script prints the command for the next step at the end.
Use the demo dataset (demo_dataset/) as the running example so all sections are consistent. Do not introduce a different example dataset without agreement.
Make randomness reproducible: expose a --seed (default 2026).
Assume genome build GRCh38.






Write narrative in Markdown.
Cite as provisional placeholders: [DOI/PMID] in square brackets, highlighted yellow. Final formatting will be harmonised to Vancouver style by the editors.
Keep figures in docs/ (PNG/PDF, 300 dpi).






Raw or intermediate genotype data (*.bed/bim/fam, *.pgen/pvar/psam, *.vcf*, downloaded HAPNEST files). These are large and are regenerated by the scripts. The .gitignore already excludes them.
Any real, access-controlled individual-level data (e.g. dbGaP / PANSCAN). The demo example uses only the synthetic HAPNEST data.
Credentials, tokens, absolute local paths.

Commit only: scripts, Markdown text, final summary statistics, and figures.




Open a GitHub Issue for anything that needs group discussion (scope of a section, an overlap between sections, a data question). Use Issues rather than email threads so the decision is visible to everyone and stays with the code.

title: How to carry out a Genome-Wide Association Study
text:
NoteAbout this guide



This is the companion website to the methodology manuscript developed within the TRANSPAN COST Action (CA21116), Working Group 1, targeted at XXXX Journal. It pairs annotated PLINK 2 and R code with a fully open, reproducible demo dataset, and is written for Master’s students and clinicians without a bioinformatics background.

title: How to carry out a Genome-Wide Association Study
text:
What is a GWAS?
A genome-wide association study (GWAS) tests the statistical association between genetic variants — typically single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) — and a trait across the entire genome, in order to identify genetic factors that contribute to complex traits and diseases.

title: How to carry out a Genome-Wide Association Study
text:
Why pancreatic cancer?
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the deliberate case study throughout this guide: a relativelly rare, multifactorial cancer/trait with a poorly characterised genetic component. Single-centre studies are underpowered, and international consortia (PanScan, PanC4, PANDoRA) are the rule rather than the exception. Teaching GWAS under these realistically difficult conditions makes the methodological decisions more transparent than a large, well-powered textbook example would.

title: How to carry out a Genome-Wide Association Study
text:
How to use this guide
Every analysis step is shown as a real command you can run yourself on the open demo dataset, so you can reproduce the entire workflow from raw genotypes to final results.
👉 Start here: Before you start — setup and your first PLINK command






TipNo coding experience?



You do not need to know how to program. Every command is given in full, with an explanation of what it does and what the output should look like. If you can copy, paste and press Enter, you can follow this guide.
